topic.title: Nervous and hormonal communication, the CNS, voluntary and reflex actions
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Short recall marks scattered through a nervous-system question rather than a block of its own. Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q4 asked for the difference in speed between the hormonal and nervous systems [1] and for an effector [1] alongside plant hormones; March 2026 set the effector as a labelling task on the Higher reflex question, where it went badly. Expect [1] marks for the CNS, the effector and the speed comparison, and [2] for a voluntary/reflex difference.
mustMemorise: Nervous: electrical impulses along neurones, fast, short-lived
Hormonal: chemical hormones in the blood, slower, longer-lasting
CNS = brain + spinal cord; it controls and co-ordinates responses
An effector is a muscle or a gland — never the stimulus, a nerve or the body part
Voluntary: conscious control, slower. Reflex: automatic, much faster
notOnThisSpec: The spinal reflex arc pathway, which is outcome 1.6.4 and Higher Tier
The structure of a neurone, myelin, and how a synapse transmits
Named hormones beyond those used as examples elsewhere in §1.6

note.title: Nervous and hormonal communication, the CNS, voluntary and reflex actions
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Nervous: impulses along neurones, fast, short-lived. Hormonal: chemicals in the blood, slower, longer-lasting
CNS = brain + spinal cord, which co-ordinates the response
Voluntary = conscious and slower; reflex = automatic and faster

mustBeAbleTo: Name the two organs of the central nervous system and say what it does
Write the five-stage pathway in order
Name the receptor and the effector in an unfamiliar situation
Say that an effector is a muscle or a gland, and why the hand or the pin is not one
Compare the two systems on speed, on what carries the message and on how long the effect lasts
Distinguish voluntary from reflex using conscious control and speed
Explain why an automatic response is faster and what that speed is for
Turn two response times into 'how many times longer' by dividing
sheet.howExamined: B1 is 1 hour: 60 marks at Foundation, 70 at Higher, calculator allowed. This topic supplies short recall parts inside a longer nervous-system or hormones question — name an effector [1], state the speed difference [1], name the parts of the CNS [1]-[2], give a voluntary/reflex difference [1]-[2] — and occasionally the paper's 6-mark QWC. Every comparison mark needs both sides named: the schemes treat a single-sided statement as a description, not a comparison.
traps: Labelling the pin, a nerve or the hand as the effector instead of the muscle (March 2026 B1 H Q6(b)(i))
Including the nerves in the central nervous system
Saying the hormonal system is faster
Giving 'different' or 'quicker' without naming both systems
Swapping the speeds of voluntary and reflex actions
Saying the CNS detects the stimulus — that is the receptor's job
Putting effector before receptor in the pathway
Subtracting when a question asks how many times longer

Offering a vague explanation where a named substance or structure is wanted: this part drew many vague answers beside the excellent ones, and 'photosynthesis' or a guessed hormone earned nothing (Summer 2025 B1 F Q4)

workedExamples.stem:
A person is startled by a loud noise. Their ear detects the sound, and a moment later their neck muscles turn their head.
(a) Name the receptor and the effector in this response. [2]
(b) The adrenal gland also releases a hormone, which makes the heart beat faster for several minutes afterwards.
Compare the nervous response with the hormonal response. [3]

figure.alt: Five boxes joined by arrows: stimulus, receptor, central nervous system, effector and response.

steps.working: Receptor: the sound receptor in the ear.
steps.decision: A receptor detects the stimulus. Naming the organ is usually enough, but saying what it detects makes the answer safe.
The effector is what carries out the response, and on this specification it is always a muscle or a gland. Not the head, which is the body part that moves.

options: Because an effector is a muscle or a gland
Because the head is too big to be an effector
Because muscles are faster than glands
whyMenu.explain: March 2026 examiners saw the pin, the hand and individual nerves all given as effectors. Muscle or gland, every time.

steps.working: The nervous response is faster than the hormonal one.
steps.decision: Speed first — the outcome names it. Say faster than what: a comparison needs both systems on the page.

steps.working: The nervous message is an electrical impulse along a neurone; the hormonal message is a chemical carried in the blood.
steps.decision: That is the 'nature of the response' the outcome asks for. Two halves again, one for each system.

steps.working: The nervous effect is short-lived, while the hormonal effect lasts for several minutes.
steps.decision: Use the detail in the stem. The question gave you 'several minutes' precisely so that you could use it.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Receptor: the sound receptor in the ear. Effector: the neck muscle. (b) The nervous response is faster than the hormonal one; it is carried as an electrical impulse along neurones rather than as a chemical in the blood; and its effect is short-lived, while the hormone's effect lasts several minutes.

twin.stem: Give two differences between the way a nervous message and a hormonal message travel through the body.

accepted: nerve impulses are electrical and travel along neurones, while hormones are chemicals carried in the blood

items.stem: Which two organs make up the central nervous system?

options.text: the brain and the spinal cord
options.feedback: Those two only. Everything else is a nerve running to or from them.
The nerves carry messages to and from the CNS but are not part of it. The CNS is the brain and the spinal cord.

options.text: the brain, the spinal cord and the heart
options.feedback: The heart is an organ the nervous system controls, not part of the system itself.
Those sit at the two ends of the pathway. The CNS is the co-ordinator in the middle.

items.stem: A pin pricks a finger and the arm muscle contracts to pull the hand away. What is the effector?
items.skill: Identify the effector in a pathway

options.feedback: The effector carries out the response, and on this specification it is always a muscle or a gland.
The pin is the stimulus. March 2026 examiners reported seeing the pin labelled as the effector.
The hand is the body part that moves. What moves it is the muscle, and that is the effector.
A neurone is part of the pathway, not the thing that responds.

items.stem: Which statement correctly compares the two communication systems?
items.skill: Compare speed and nature of response

options.text: The nervous system is faster but its effects are shorter-lived than the hormonal system's
options.feedback: Both halves named, both directions right. That is a comparison.

options.text: The hormonal system is faster and its effects last longer
options.feedback: Hormones travel in the blood, which is much slower than an impulse along a neurone. The longer-lasting half is right.

options.text: The nervous system is faster and its effects last longer
options.feedback: Faster is right, but nervous effects are short-lived. The hormonal ones last longer.

options.text: They work at the same speed but in different parts of the body
options.feedback: The speed difference is exactly what the outcome asks you to know.

items.stem: Which pair correctly describes a reflex action?

options.feedback: Not under conscious control, and faster than a voluntary action — the two things the outcome names.
A reflex happens before you have decided anything. Conscious control belongs to voluntary actions.

options.text: automatic and slower than a voluntary action
options.feedback: Automatic is right, but the speed is the other way round. Reflexes are fast, which is the point of them.

options.text: controlled by hormones rather than nerves
options.feedback: A reflex is a nervous response. Hormones are the other communication system.

context.setting: An introduction to a nervous-system question

figures.alt: Five boxes joined by arrows: stimulus, receptor, central nervous system, effector and response. The organs of the central nervous system are not named.

parts.stem: Name the two organs that make up the central nervous system.

accepted: the brain and the spinal cord

scheme.for: brain
spinal cord

hints: Two organs, and neither of them is a nerve.
parts.workedSolution: The brain and the spinal cord.

commonErrors.feedback: Nerves carry messages to and from the CNS but are not part of it. The CNS is the brain and the spinal cord.

parts.stem: State the function of the central nervous system.

accepted: it controls and co-ordinates the responses between receptors and effectors

scheme.for: controls and co-ordinates the response between receptors and effectors

hints: The specification uses one particular verb for what the CNS does.
parts.workedSolution: It controls and co-ordinates the responses between the receptors and the effectors.

commonErrors.feedback: Detecting is the receptor's job. The CNS co-ordinates what happens next.

context.setting: A student stepping on a sharp stone in bare feet

figures.alt: Five boxes joined by arrows: stimulus, a box marked A, central nervous system, a box marked B, and response. A and B are not named.

parts.stem:
Complete the pathway by writing the missing words.

stimulus  →  ______  →  central nervous system  →  ______  →  response

scheme.for: receptor
effector

hints: Something detects the change, and something else carries out the response.
parts.workedSolution: stimulus → receptor → central nervous system → effector → response.

commonErrors.feedback: The two are the wrong way round. The receptor detects first; the effector acts last.

parts.stem: Name the effector when the student lifts their foot off the stone.

scheme.for: (leg) muscle
scheme.examinerNote: March 2026: the pin, the hand and individual nerves were all seen as incorrect answers for the effector.

hints: An effector is always a muscle or a gland on this specification.
parts.workedSolution: A muscle in the leg — it contracts to lift the foot.

commonErrors.feedback: The foot is the body part that moves and the stone is the stimulus. The effector is the muscle that does the moving.

parts.stem: Name the receptor in this response.

scheme.for: pain / touch / pressure receptor in the skin

hints: Which part of the body met the stone first?
parts.workedSolution: A pain or pressure receptor in the skin of the foot.

context.setting: A comparison of the two communication systems in a revision table

figures.alt: A table naming four features, what carries the message, how it travels, the speed of response and how long the effect continues, with the nervous system and hormonal system columns left blank.

parts.stem: State the difference, if any, in the speed of response between the hormonal system and the nervous system.

scheme.for: the hormonal response is slower (than the nervous response)

hints: Hormones travel in the blood. Impulses travel along neurones.
parts.workedSolution: The hormonal response is slower than the nervous response.

commonErrors.feedback: The hormonal system is the slower of the two, because the blood takes time to carry hormones around the body.

parts.stem: Give two other differences between the nervous and hormonal systems.

accepted: nerve impulses are electrical and travel along neurones while hormones are chemicals carried in the blood; nervous effects are short-lived while hormonal effects last longer

scheme.for: any two from: nervous uses electrical impulses along neurones, hormonal uses chemicals in the blood / nervous effects are short-lived, hormonal effects are longer-lasting — [1] each
scheme.examinerNote: Each difference must name both systems (research 03 §7.1).

hints: Two rows of the table besides speed: what carries the message, and how long the effect lasts.
parts.workedSolution: Nerve impulses are electrical and travel along neurones, while hormones are chemicals carried in the blood. Nervous effects are short-lived, while hormonal effects last longer.

commonErrors.feedback: Only one system has been described. A difference names both and says how they differ.

context.setting: Two everyday actions: catching a falling glass and blinking

figures.alt: A table comparing a voluntary action with a reflex action on three features: control and speed, both left blank, and an example of each, picking up a pen and blinking at dust.

parts.stem: Give two ways a voluntary action differs from a reflex action.

accepted: a voluntary action is under conscious control while a reflex is automatic; a reflex is faster than a voluntary action

scheme.for: a voluntary action is under conscious control; a reflex action is automatic / not consciously controlled
a reflex action is faster than a voluntary action
scheme.examinerNote: The outcome names conscious control and speed of response, so those are the two points.

hints: The outcome tells you which two things to mention.
Each difference needs both sides described.
parts.workedSolution: A voluntary action is consciously controlled — you decide to do it — while a reflex action is automatic and not under conscious control. A reflex action is also much faster than a voluntary one.

commonErrors.feedback: The speeds are the wrong way round. A reflex is fast precisely because the brain is not making a decision.

parts.stem: Explain why it is useful that a reflex action is not under conscious control.

accepted: it happens faster, so it protects the body from harm before you have time to think

scheme.for: the response happens faster because no conscious decision is needed
so the body is protected from harm / damage

hints: Two ideas: what skipping the decision does to the speed, and what that speed is for.
parts.workedSolution: Because no conscious decision has to be made, the response happens much faster, which protects the body from damage — you have pulled your hand off a hot pan before you have noticed the pain.

context.setting: A class timing two kinds of response in a science lesson

data.caption: Mean response times measured by a class

parts.stem:
Use the table to calculate how many times longer the voluntary response took than the reflex.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: 'How many times' is a ratio, so the answer has no unit.

hints: 'How many times longer' means divide, not subtract.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.20 s is how much longer, not how many times longer. 'How many times' asks for a division.

parts.stem: Explain why the reflex response is the faster of the two.

accepted: the reflex does not involve a conscious decision by the brain, so the pathway is shorter

scheme.for: a reflex is automatic and needs no conscious decision
so the impulse travels a shorter pathway / passes through fewer connections before reaching the effector

hints: What does a voluntary action have to do that a reflex skips?
parts.workedSolution: A reflex is automatic, so no conscious decision has to be made in the brain. The impulse therefore travels a shorter and more direct pathway to the effector, which makes the response much quicker.

context.setting: Two responses in the same person: jumping at a bang, and growing taller over a year

parts.stem:
One response happens in a fraction of a second; another takes place slowly over a whole year.
Suggest which communication system controls each, and give a reason for each answer.

accepted: the fast response is nervous because impulses travel quickly along neurones; the slow one is hormonal because hormones travel in the blood and their effects last a long time

scheme.for: the fast response is controlled by the nervous system
because nerve impulses travel very quickly along neurones and the effect is short-lived
the slow, year-long change is controlled by the hormonal system
because hormones are carried more slowly in the blood and their effects are long-lasting

hints: Match the timescale of the response to the timescale of the system.
Each answer needs a reason, and the reason should mention how the message travels.
parts.workedSolution: Jumping at a bang is nervous: impulses travel very quickly along neurones and the effect is over in a moment. Growing taller over a year is hormonal: hormones are carried in the blood, which is slower, and their effects are long-lasting.

commonErrors.feedback: Hormones are the slower route. Match the fast response to the nervous system.

context.setting: A cyclist braking when a car pulls out, and then feeling shaky for minutes afterwards

figures.alt: Five boxes joined by arrows: stimulus, receptor, a blank box that co-ordinates the response, effector and response.

parts.stem:
The cyclist sees the car and squeezes the brakes.
Name the receptor and the effector in this response.

accepted: light receptors in the eye and a muscle in the hand or arm

scheme.for: receptor: light receptor in the eye / the eye
effector: a muscle (in the hand or arm)
scheme.examinerNote: March 2026: the pin, nerves and the hand were all seen as incorrect effectors.

hints: The effector is a muscle or a gland — nothing else counts.
parts.workedSolution: Receptor: the light receptors in the eye. Effector: a muscle in the hand or arm, which contracts to squeeze the brake.

commonErrors.feedback: The hand is the body part; the brake is the object. The effector is the muscle that moves them.

parts.stem: State the part of the body that co-ordinates this response.

scheme.for: the central nervous system (the brain)

parts.workedSolution: The central nervous system — here, the brain.

parts.stem:
Squeezing the brakes is a voluntary action.
Give one way in which a voluntary action differs from a reflex action.

accepted: a voluntary action is under conscious control whereas a reflex is automatic

scheme.for: a voluntary action is under conscious control (a reflex is automatic) / a voluntary action is slower than a reflex
scheme.examinerNote: Either of the two features named by the outcome is accepted.

hints: The outcome names two features: conscious control and speed.
parts.workedSolution: A voluntary action is consciously controlled, while a reflex action is automatic — and a reflex is also faster.

parts.stem:
For several minutes afterwards the cyclist's heart is still beating fast because a hormone has been released into the blood.
Explain why the effect of the hormone lasts much longer than the nervous response did.

accepted: the hormone stays in the blood and is carried round the body until it is broken down, while a nerve impulse is over in an instant

scheme.for: the hormone is carried in the blood round the whole body
and remains there until it is broken down, so its effect is long-lasting, whereas a nerve impulse acts once and stops
scheme.examinerNote: A comparison needs both systems mentioned.

hints: Where is the hormone, and how long does it stay there?
parts.workedSolution: The hormone is released into the blood, which carries it round the whole body, and it stays there until it is broken down — so its effect continues for minutes. A nerve impulse, by contrast, passes along a neurone once and its effect is over almost immediately.

context.setting: A student writing a revision summary of the body's two communication systems

parts.stem:
The human body has two communication systems.
Compare the nervous system with the hormonal system, and describe the part played by the central nervous system in a response.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: the nervous system carries electrical nerve impulses along neurones
the hormonal system carries chemical hormones in the blood
the nervous response is fast; the hormonal response is slower
nervous effects are short-lived; hormonal effects are longer-lasting
the central nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord
it controls and co-ordinates the response between receptors and effectors
a receptor detects the stimulus and an effector — a muscle or a gland — carries out the response

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Every comparison sentence should name both systems, or it counts once rather than twice.
Finish with the pathway: stimulus, receptor, CNS, effector, response.
parts.workedSolution: The nervous system sends electrical nerve impulses along neurones, while the hormonal system sends chemical hormones in the blood. The nervous response is fast but short-lived, whereas the hormonal response is slower but longer-lasting. The central nervous system is made up of the brain and the spinal cord. It controls and co-ordinates the body's responses: a receptor detects a stimulus and sends impulses to the central nervous system, which decides what should happen and sends impulses on to an effector — a muscle or a gland — which carries out the response.

commonErrors.feedback: Two separate descriptions are not a comparison. Each indicative point about speed or duration expects both systems in the same sentence.

findTheMistake.stem:
Órla is asked: 'A drawing pin is stepped on and the leg muscle contracts to lift the foot. Label the effector on the diagram. [1]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: She labels the foot as the effector.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The foot is the body part that moves, not the thing that produces the movement. An effector on this specification is a **muscle or a gland**, so the label belongs on the leg muscle that contracts.
correction: She labels the leg muscle as the effector.
findTheMistake.feedback: No mark, and it is the single most predictable loss in this topic: March 2026's examiners reported the pin, the hand and individual nerves all being labelled as the effector on the same question. The test that never fails is to ask 'what actually does the response?' — a muscle contracts or a gland releases something, and nothing else on the diagram can. Everything else is the stimulus, the pathway or the body part being moved.

prompts.prompt: Name the two organs of the central nervous system and say what it does.
prompts.answer: The brain and the spinal cord. It controls and co-ordinates the responses between receptors and effectors.

prompts.prompt: What is an effector, and what is it never?
prompts.answer: A muscle or a gland — the thing that carries out the response. It is never the stimulus, a nerve, or the body part that moves.

prompts.prompt: Give three differences between the nervous and hormonal systems.
prompts.answer: Nervous: electrical impulses along neurones, fast, short-lived. Hormonal: chemical hormones in the blood, slower, longer-lasting.

prompts.prompt: How do voluntary and reflex actions differ?
prompts.answer: A voluntary action is under conscious control and is slower; a reflex action is automatic, not consciously controlled, and much faster.
